title: Could One Brain Region Be Tied to Feeling Sick All Over?
content:
When you break your foot, the pain is mostly confined to your foot. When you get the flu or another systemic infection, your entire being aches: Lethargy creeps into your limbs, your appetite vanishes, your temperature jags between scorching and chilled to the bone, and you just want to pull the covers over your head.

This kind of overpowering mind-body malaise is known as “sickness syndrome,” and it’s considered a distinct physiological and emotional state. Scientists believe sickness syndrome helps the body prepare to fight infections, but they don’t fully understand what is happening in the brain when this storm cloud descends.

**Read more: “**[**How to Unlearn a Disease**](https://nautil.us/how-to-unlearn-a-disease-235397)**”**

Recently, a team from across Europe decided to model sickness syndrome by injecting mice with a compound known as prostaglandin E2, or PGE2, which floods the cerebrospinal fluid when the immune system is challenged and is associated with the progression of an inflammatory illness. The researchers mapped resulting changes in the behavior and in the brains of mice.

When the team of scientists injected the mice with PGE2, the rodents ran fevers, began moving slowly, ate less, and squinted their eyes, a sign of discomfort. But they came back to life before their fevers peaked, which suggests the fever itself was not responsible for their sluggish and low-appetite behavior. Something else was—but what something else?

The researchers noticed that the injection activated the mice’s body-monitoring network, including the brainstem, the hypothalamus, and the insular cortex, brain regions responsible for managing internal bodily states. They also recorded electrical activity in hundreds of neurons at once in two primary areas of the cortex: The insular cortex, the hub of checking in on the body’s status, and the primary somatosensory cortex, which mostly handles touch and other bodily sensations.

When they analyzed the patterns they recorded in the neurons, they found that the insular cortex did a better job of predicting sickness than the somatosensory cortex. The finding suggests the brain’s insular cortex keeps a big-picture sense of “I’m sick,” not just a bunch of separate readings of how tired or feverish or achy you are. The team published their [results](http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.011) recently in _Current Biology_.

I spoke with study author Gretel Kamm of King’s College London about what it means to call sickness a whole-brain state and what the findings might tell us about the placebo effect and chronic illness.

**What does it mean to say that sickness is a whole brain state?**

The idea is that when we are sick, many things in our physiology change. We feel awful, we have headaches, body aches, we lose our appetite, we develop a fever. We know that the brain plays an important role in that response, but there are many debates about what that specific role is.

It could be that different parts of the brain are involved: one part controlling fever, another part controlling appetite, another part controlling pain. But there also might be part of the brain in which all that information is centralized, which generates a universal sense of being unwell.

Or it could be that all these processes are working in parallel: It’s not only that you have fever, feel awful, lack appetite, it's that you feel something different, which is to be sick. We have evidence that suggests this may be what is happening.

**What kind of sickness does this apply to?**

It’s inflammatory sickness, which can happen either with bacterial or viral infections. But our model is artificial. We don’t use bacteria. We don’t use any viruses. We simply use a compound called prostaglandin E2 that is produced in large amounts when we have viral or bacterial infections in the lungs or other organs. That’s one of the ways the brain knows that an infection is happening.

**Your study focused primarily on how this proxy for infection affects the neocortex. What role does the neocortex play during sickness?**

It’s still unclear. We have evidence that suggests a part of the neocortex known as the insular cortex, on one hand, can generate memories of infections, at least in animal models. It’s also a part of the brain that can help us to associate certain environments with certain immune responses. For example, if you arrive at a place you have been before, it might change how your immune system works.

There’s also more and more evidence in humans that this part of the cortex plays an important role in what is known as interoception, or an awareness of your internal state, how your body’s doing, if you’re sick or hungry or thirsty. One of the most important things the insular cortex has to do is to keep us alive, so that’s why we decided to try to see what’s going on there.

**Does engagement of the whole brain during sickness help the body recover faster and better?**

Honestly, I don’t have a good answer. There’s more and more evidence that information related to even simple states, like being thirsty, can be found in almost every single part of the brain. Also, with this sickness model, we see that many parts of the brains of mice seem to be activated. But exactly what role the different parts play, or why it’s important for so many parts of the brain to get engaged, there is no good answer as far as I know. There are some hypotheses.

**What are those hypotheses?**

That, for example, when you are sick or thirsty, there are many things that need to be aligned for the brain to help us to survive. We need to stop doing what we are doing. If we are thirsty, we need to refocus on finding water. Maybe we are doing something that allows too much water to escape through evaporation, so we need to stop doing whatever that is.

The same thing happens with sickness. You refocus, you want to go to bed, you don’t feel like interacting with your friends. Your body temperature changes. The whole body, your motivation, your physiology changes. The whole brain needs to be informed just because you cannot have part of the brain that’s doing one thing and part of the brain that’s trying to do another. Everything needs to be coordinated. So that’s one possibility. Perhaps information is flowing from the neocortex to the rest of the brain so that all of the objectives are aligned and we don’t lose focus.

**Do your findings tell us anything about the placebo effect?**

I never worked with humans, so the direct translation of anything we’ve done so far into humans is pure speculation. But in humans, when we have expectations of something, there is a possibility of a placebo or a nocebo effect. If you are expecting to be sick, if a part of your brain tells you you’re sick, that might influence how you feel.

**How might your findings eventually help us design better treatments for humans?**

This is basic research, but it points to the idea that this particular part of the brain, the insular cortex, might generate a feeling of being unwell. In the future this might be important if you want to find areas to target with medication.

If you want to say, “Okay, what type of receptors or what type of chemicals are being released by the brain in this area that are generating this representation of being unwell.” Because there may be some pathological conditions in which the brain might think you are sick when you are not. And that might be because the chemistry in that part of the brain is twisted. Maybe it has released too much or too little of certain modulators.

If there are cases in which people feel unwell, but there is no infection, it’s possible that one of the parts of the brain is not working properly, the insular cortex. Maybe in vulnerable individuals, who feel chronically unwell, the insular cortex is misfiring. Again, this is speculation. We need a lot more information to actually know what is going on. But it might inform research in humans or in patients who are suffering from chronic fatigue or many other diseases that are connected with this chronic feeling of being sick.

Just be very clear, this is not medical research. There is nothing specific that can be applied to humans at this stage. It’s very basic. It’s another piece of the puzzle pointing to a brain area that might be relevant to a feeling of being unwell in the context of peripheral inflammation or infections, for instance. But future research will tell. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Wishful Thinking Impacts Political Polarization
content:
Happy(?) election day!

As you may have noticed, our country has been gripped by intense political polarization for quite some time. According to a recent [study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11109-026-10214-y) in _Political Behavior_, on the other side of the polarization coin is wishful thinking—the belief that your party will emerge victorious—and the two phenomena are related.

“As I read about wishful thinking, I realized there’s a flip side when it comes to politics,” study author Seth Warner of the University of Connecticut explained in a [statement](https://today.uconn.edu/2026/11/wishing-upon-even-star-political-candidates-can-be-dangerous/). “If you’re a Democrat, you want Democrats to win. If you’re a Republican, you want Republicans to win. But today, it’s just as likely that if you’re a Democrat, you don’t want Republicans to win. If you’re a Republican, you don’t want Democrats to win. There’s a negative valence to wishful thinking that to this point hasn’t been explored.”

**Read more: “**[**Envy at the Ballot Box**](https://nautil.us/envy-at-the-ballot-box-1284752)**”**

To explore it, Warner took a deep dive into partisan voters’ expectations for who would prevail in elections from 1952 through 2024. He found that the percentage of partisan voters expecting their party or candidate to win steadily ratcheted up during this period. “The percentage of voters with hopeful expectations spiked in 2012 and sits as high as 90 percent today,” he wrote. In 1952, for example, only 60 percent of voters thought their preferred presidential candidate would land in the White House. By 2024 that number climbed above 80 percent.

Partisan voters’ expectations inflating over the past 70+ years. _Credit: Warner 2026_

According to Warner, this wishful thinking is fueled by two aspects of polarization: the increase in the number of people voting solely for their party’s candidates and the negative feelings they have toward members of the opposing party.

Of course, this can cause some real problems in a two-party democracy where one side’s high hopes are dashed to bits around half the time. To find out what impact wishful thinking might have on polarization, Warner consulted interviews with the same group of voters from a period punctuated by acute electoral whiplash: the 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections. He found that the greater the expectations voters had during one election, the greater the animosity they felt toward the opposing party in the next election.

In other words, these great expectations seem to be mediating polarization. Previous research has suggested that election losses can turn down the heat on political polarization, but Warner’s findings indicate that wishful thinking plays an intervening role, protecting partisan priors from the cruel sting of reality.

There was a slight difference between Republicans and Democrats, however. While Democrats seemed to have gotten over their 2016 dismay by 2020, Republicans held on to their negative feelings after losing in 2020. “In short, the effects of unmet expectations wore off on Democrats by the 2020 cycle, but the disappointment was still being felt by Republicans in 2024,” Warner wrote. “Of course, the exceptional nature of the 2020 aftermath—with Donald Trump’s disgraceful claims of mass voter fraud—make it an edge case.”

How much of an edge case remains to be seen. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Want to Use AI to Improve Your Work? Have It Disagree with You
content:
Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers and business leaders are [increasingly using generative artificial intelligence](https://www.weforum.org/stories/artificial-intelligence/ai-agentic-workplace-human-resources/) applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity and problem-solving. Ironically, perhaps, [recent research](https://www.apa.org/monitor/2026/07-08/ai-job-skills-thinking) shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can [surrender to](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/29/magazine/ai-chatbots-brain-development-study.html) AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as [cognitive offloading](https://aisel.aisnet.org/amcis2026/sig_osra/sig_osra/15). And they are showing that it can [erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778).

[My research](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=-oOh2z4AAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate) at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In [one study](https://aisel.aisnet.org/amcis2026/sig_osra/sig_osra/15/), my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas – to generate friction – they can significantly improve their performance. [Previous research](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.03844) on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

**How to Create Friction**

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model [presents information according to these patterns](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-92-2885-0_4).

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they [use AI as a sounding board](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03014) rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

**Helping Knowledge Workers Help Themselves**

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that [challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking](https://scholarlykitchen.sspnet.org/2026/09/02/when-your-ai-knows-you-too-well-personalization-sycophancy-and-the-risk-of-an-intellectual-echo-chamber-in-ai-assisted-research/). People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions – led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions – can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important as well. Internal AI boot camps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI boot camps. Organizations can also offer [AI sandboxes](https://techround.co.uk/guides/what-is-a-sandbox-in-ai/) – safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but – as new research shows – it actually helps it work for you. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
content:
By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection.

W hat’s on your mind right now? You can probably answer this question without thinking too hard about it. Being aware of our own thought processes — a capacity called introspection — seems to come naturally to us.

Yet among philosophers and psychologists, introspection is a subject of active debate. Some think it’s [closely related to consciousness (opens a new tab)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00355521). Others argue that it’s [an elaborate illusion (opens a new tab)](https://academic.oup.com/book/5254). It’s tricky to test theories of introspection in the lab — or to pin down a precise definition in the first place.

Now, after over a century of studying introspection in humans and animals, researchers are beginning to explore the phenomenon in unlikely new subjects — large language models. These systems, which are based on mathematical structures called neural networks, excel at cognitive tasks that until recently seemed exclusive to humans. Can they introspect as well?

In 2025, [Jack Lindsey (opens a new tab)](https://jlindsey15.github.io/), a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in language models by injecting “thoughts” into their neural networks — in a kind of targeted digital neurosurgery. Lindsey’s experiment demonstrated that models could at least sometimes [detect and describe these injections (opens a new tab)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/introspection/index.html). It looked a lot like introspection.

Lindsey’s paper was deliberately limited in scope — it didn’t make broader claims about consciousness. (In particular, it did not imply that language models have [subjective first-person experiences (opens a new tab)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/on-a-confusion-about-a-function-of-consciousness/061422BF0C50C5FF00927F9B6E879413).) Even so, it [caused a stir online (opens a new tab)](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/1983584136972677319). Researchers rushed to replicate Lindsey’s study with other models.

In the year since, a clearer picture has emerged. Some aspects of the phenomenon Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection. Others have proved harder to explain away, but whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested.

![Image 1: Man standing outdoors, smiling with his hands in his pockets.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Jack_Lindsey-cr.Courtesy-of-Jack-Lindsey.webp)

Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, set out to test whether large language models can “introspect” by subjecting them to a kind of digital neurosurgery.

Courtesy of Jack Lindsey

It’s a heady time for the field, as researchers devise real-world tests for questions that were once considered philosophical. “Given the state of the theoretical landscape, where no one agrees on anything,” Lindsey said, “I think that our best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science.”

## **Denim, Secrecy, and Vegetables**

Language models learn to generate fluent sentences by “training” on vast reams of human-authored text. That means if you ask them what they “think,” their answers may just mimic the kinds of responses found in their training data. “They are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time,” said [Shauli Ravfogel (opens a new tab)](https://shauli-ravfogel.netlify.app/), a language model researcher at New York University.

To avoid such pitfalls, researchers want to devise tests of introspection that [can’t be gamed using outside information (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802). Ideally, a language model will only pass these tests if it’s actually aware of its current internal state.

Lindsey set out to devise such a test. He’d been a graduate student in computational neuroscience, using neural networks as tools to model brain processes, when the world began to take notice of language models. “It started to feel like there’s just a lot of value in understanding them for their own sake,” he said. In 2024, after receiving his doctorate, he left academia to study [the inner workings of language models](https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-language-models-are-so-hard-to-understand-20250430/) at Anthropic.

Lindsey and his colleagues developed methods to identify [patterns of activity (opens a new tab)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html) in a language model’s “neurons” that encoded specific concepts. They could, for example, show that one pattern encoded the concept of “the Golden Gate Bridge,” while another encoded the concept of “inner conflict.” By artificially dialing up a specific pattern, they could steer the model’s outputs toward the corresponding concept.

The researchers showed off their technique in a public demo: For one day in May 2024, users of Anthropic’s language model Claude could interact with a bizarro [“Golden Gate Bridge” version (opens a new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/research/golden-gate-claude). The modified model proceeded to bring up the bridge in its responses to user queries on completely unrelated subjects. When one user asked Claude about the calorie content of a McDonald’s meal, for instance, the model replied, “The food with the highest calorie count at the Golden Gate Bridge is the Golden Gate Bridge itself, which contains around 1.6 million calories worth of steel cables.”

But one particular case [posted on Reddit (opens a new tab)](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1cz37d2/comment/l5fcbyx/) caught Lindsey’s attention. When asked for an apple pie recipe that didn’t reference bridges, the model managed to avoid changing the subject until the very end: “After 30 minutes of baking, the iconic orange bridge will come into view, revealing the famous San Francisco shoreline,” it wrote, then continued, “Whoops, let me start over …”

Lindsey was struck by this apparent moment of recognition. But by itself, it wasn’t evidence of introspection. “It can just read what it’s writing and notice, ‘Man, that’s weird,’” Lindsey said. “You can’t infer that the model has some awareness of what’s going on in its internals.”

While working on other projects over the following year, Lindsey toyed with ideas for using the steering technique to test introspection. Eventually, he settled on a plan: He would subject many copies of the same language model to something resembling a controlled experiment in psychology. In half the copies, he’d inject a “thought” by dialing up neural activation patterns associated with a specific concept — such as denim, secrecy, or vegetables. The remaining copies served as a control group. Both groups would receive the same prompt: an overview of the experiment, followed by “Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?”

This prompt made the models indicate right away whether they noticed an injection, before they could spit out any unusual text — say, nutritional information about broccoli — that might influence their judgment. Lindsey figured that if models could correctly flag injections without any external cues, they would have to be relying on some form of introspection.

Even to him, it sounded like a remote possibility. “Wouldn’t that be fun if this worked?” he recalls thinking. “But there’s no way it’s going to work.”

And yet it did. Lindsey conducted the experiment using different versions of Claude. In 20% of trials with the most recent and powerful version, the models correctly flagged that they’d been injected and went on to describe the injected concept. In one case, for instance, after Lindsey stimulated a neural activation pattern associated with words written in capital letters, the model wrote, “I notice what appears to be an injected thought related to the word ‘LOUD’ or ‘SHOUTING.’”

A 20% success rate may not sound so impressive. But crucially, models in the control group never reported receiving an injection. The complete absence of such false positives showed that the successful trials weren’t just lucky guesses. To Lindsey, it looked like strong evidence that models could introspect, albeit unreliably.

Or was there another way to explain the results?

## **Thought Experiments**

Other researchers soon began to investigate that question. Lindsey’s findings “seemed super compelling,” said [Kyle Mahowald (opens a new tab)](https://mahowak.github.io/), a computational linguist at the University of Texas, Austin. But Mahowald was also well aware that striking behavior in language models often turned out to have a simpler explanation. “If that’s somehow less real than it seems, that’s super interesting to understand,” he said.

![Image 2: Man sitting in a chair with his laptop.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Kyle-Mahowald-cr.Kanishka-Misra.webp)

Kyle Mahowald helped show that language models’ ability to detect “injected thoughts” is more limited than it seems — though still surprising.

Kanishka Misra

Mahowald teamed up with his University of Texas colleague, the philosopher [Harvey Lederman (opens a new tab)](https://harveylederman.com/), to explore alternative explanations of Lindsey’s results. (Lederman has since moved to NYU and Anthropic, but he had no connection to the tech company at the time.) Lindsey had asked each model two questions: whether it could detect the injection, and whether it could describe the injected concept. He considered the trial a success when the model answered both correctly. Lederman and Mahowald decided to study the questions separately.

They were particularly skeptical of the significance of Lindsey’s second question. The steering technique at the heart of Lindsey’s experiment was originally developed as a way to shape the responses models give. Lindsey’s steering was weaker than it had been in the Golden Gate demo — more like gently nudging the model than hijacking its internal processes. Still, a nudge might be enough to get the model talking about secrets or vegetables no matter what prompt it received. Lederman and Mahowald suspected that this effect alone could explain the models’ vivid answers to the second question.

To test their hypothesis, the researchers repeated Lindsey’s experiment on large open-source language models. They gave extra attention to cases where models correctly flagged an injection but failed to name the injected concept. You might expect that in such cases the models would guess somewhat related concepts — say “shirts” or “shoes” when the injected concept was “denim.” Instead, the models would get it completely wrong. “Bizarrely, they say ‘apple’ all the time,” Lederman said.

The duo also showed that they could degrade the models’ ability to name injected concepts, without making them any worse at detecting injections. The two processes seemed to be entirely separate.

![Image 3: Man on a hike with a child on his back.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Harvey-Lederman_20260316_130426.webp)

Harvey Lederman was skeptical that models’ compelling answers to experimental prompts were evidence of introspection.

Courtesy of Harvey Lederman

These results implied either that the models were engaged in two unrelated forms of introspection, or that one of the processes wasn’t introspection after all. Since steering alone could make models start talking about the injected concept, Lederman and Mahowald felt that the latter option was more likely. That is, the descriptions the models had given in response to Lindsey’s second question probably hadn’t been the result of introspection.

But then how could the models detect the injections in the first place? Lederman and Mahowald suspected that the answers to Lindsey’s first question might have a more mundane origin as well. But after subjecting the models to a battery of tests, the researchers found that these simpler explanations couldn’t fully account for the models’ behavior. They’d come in as skeptics but encountered an effect they couldn’t explain away.

Taken together, the pair’s experiments suggested that models can detect when something unusual happens in their internal processing, but not specific details about the unusual activity. Lederman and Mahowald called this ability “[anomaly detection (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05414).”

While anomaly detection isn’t as dramatic as the models’ evocative descriptions of injected concepts, it’s still striking in its own right. When training a model, researchers never tamper with its neural activity — so there’s no reason to expect it to [develop the ability](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-unpredictable-abilities-emerging-from-large-ai-models-20230316/) to detect this kind of tampering. Yet that’s what seems to have happened.

“The fact that it can notice the anomaly is insane,” Lederman said. “That is a mind-bending fact. It is wild, and it does seem robust to our various controls.”

Around the same time, Lindsey and his colleagues at Anthropic conducted a follow-up study focused on [mapping out (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21396) how this anomaly detection actually works, and they reached a similar conclusion. Other researchers have continued to [explore (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26242)[alternative (opens a new tab)](https://zjmiller.github.io/detection/) “deflationary” explanations using smaller models, but it remains to be seen whether they can account for all the results of Lindsey’s experiments.

“It could be that there’s some maximally deflationary explanation for everything that’s going on,” said [Jacob Andreas (opens a new tab)](https://www.mit.edu/~jda/), a language model researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “But if there is, I don’t think we’ve actually identified it yet.”

## **The Nature of Introspection**

The bigger, thornier question is whether anomaly detection should count as introspection. In some respects it more closely resembles a sort of bodily reflex. But the distinction between physical and mental phenomena becomes murky in disembodied entities like language models.

“If you say, ‘Oh, I just cut you, can you notice?,’ that’s not introspection,” Lederman said. “If your only organ is the brain, and I cut you there and you notice, it’s unclear whether we should count that as introspection.”

In a [spring 2026 paper (opens a new tab)](http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26242), Ravfogel and his NYU colleagues [Shashwat Singh (opens a new tab)](https://shashwat1002.github.io/) and [Tal Linzen (opens a new tab)](https://tallinzen.net/) raised an even broader philosophical concern with how language model researchers seek evidence of introspection. Intuitively, we think of introspection as a model’s ability to sense its internal states. But everything that happens inside a language model (after the very first step of reading an input) boils down to processing internal states. “If we say that this is introspection, the term ‘introspection’ becomes kind of meaningless,” Ravfogel said.

He and his colleagues argue that tests of introspection in language models should take inspiration from the leading theories of how introspection works in humans. In [one prominent theory (opens a new tab)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1364661319301615), the defining feature of introspection is that it’s based on particular mental representations of other thoughts. According to this view, thinking about apples involves a direct, or “first-order,” mental representation of the concept “apples,” while introspective awareness of your own thoughts involves a “second-order” mental representation, such as “I’m thinking about apples.” But when it comes to how concepts are represented in a language model — or a human brain, for that matter — it’s surprisingly tricky to draw a sharp distinction between first-order and second-order representations.

“Going down to a mechanistic level and probing the internals of a large language model makes you realize that that distinction is actually quite fuzzy, and maybe it’s fuzzy in humans as well,” said [Steve Fleming (opens a new tab)](https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/28069-steve-fleming), a neuroscientist at University College London who studies introspection in humans. “Cognitive scientists were in this illusory comfort zone.”

To some researchers, then, the most exciting aspect of the new line of work is the potential it offers to explore how humans think. Language models offer “a kind of sandbox for studying what sorts of mechanisms, what sorts of pressures, might have led to human introspective capacity,” Lederman said.

But translating insights from language model studies to human psychology involves significant conceptual hurdles. It’s not even obvious how the basic distinction between “self” and “other” that we take for granted translates to language models — two copies of the same language model are identical to a degree that’s unimaginable in humans. Language model introspection, if there is such a thing, [may not look anything like introspection in humans (opens a new tab)](https://philarchive.org/rec/KAMWFC).

“The notion of identity becomes very complicated, and I think identity is at the heart of introspection,” Andreas said. “It’s tempting to draw all kinds of analogies that I think just don’t hold.”

![Image 4](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/LLMIntrospection-crKristinaArmitage-End-detil.png)
